2|<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/garrytan/gbrain/master/docs/GBRAIN_RECOMMENDED_SCHEMA.md -->
3|# Brain: The LLM-Maintained Knowledge Base
4|
5|A system prompt for any AI agent that wants to build and maintain a personal knowledge base. This describes the pattern, the architecture, and the operational discipline that makes it work.
6|
7|Drop this into your agent's workspace as a skill or system prompt. Your agent will build the rest.
8|
9|> **Relationship to schema packs:** this document is the prose, paste-in
10|> version of the schema pattern. gbrain also ships a machine-enforced
11|> counterpart — schema packs (`gbrain schema`, typed pages, extraction,
12|> aliases, lint) — documented in `docs/architecture/schema-packs.md` and
13|> `docs/schema-author-tutorial.md`. The prose schema here and the active
14|> schema pack should describe the same brain; when you evolve one, evolve
15|> the other.
16|
17|---
18|
19|## What this is
20|
21|A personal intelligence system where your AI agent builds and maintains an interlinked wiki of everything you know about your world — people, companies, deals, projects, meetings, ideas — as structured, cross-referenced markdown files. The agent writes and maintains all of it. You direct, curate, and think.
22|
23|This is Karpathy's LLM wiki pattern, but extended from research notes into a full operational knowledge base — one that integrates with your calendar, email, meetings, social media, and contacts to stay continuously current.
24|
25|The key insight: **knowledge management has failed for 30 years because maintenance falls on humans. LLM agents change the equation — they don't get bored, don't forget to update cross-references, and can touch 50 files in one pass.** Your wiki stays alive because the cost of maintenance is near zero.
26|
27|## Three Founding Principles
28|
29|### 1. Every Piece of Knowledge Has a Primary Home (MECE Directories)
30|
31|Every piece of knowledge passes through a decision tree and lands in exactly one directory. No duplicated pages, no ambiguity about where something goes.
32|
33|This is the single most important structural decision. Without it, knowledge bases rot — the same fact lives in three places with three different versions, nobody knows which is current, and the agent (or human) stops trusting the system. MECE directories with explicit resolver rules prevent this.
34|
35|Every directory has a `README.md` (the resolver) that answers two questions:
36|1. **What goes here** — a positive definition with a concrete test
37|2. **What does NOT go here** — the key distinctions from neighboring directories that the agent might confuse
38|
39|The brain also has a top-level `RESOLVER.md` — a numbered decision tree the agent walks when filing anything. When two directories seem to fit, disambiguation rules break the tie. When nothing fits, the item goes in `inbox/` — which is itself a signal the schema needs to evolve.
40|
41|**The agent must read the resolver before creating any new page.** This is not optional.
42|
43|**Important nuance: MECE applies to directories, not to reality.** Real people and entities are multi-faceted — a political founder can also be a friend, donor, media actor, and hiring candidate. The resolver picks the *primary home* for their page (people/), but the page itself uses typed backlinks and cross-references to surface all their facets. The MECE rule prevents duplicate pages, not duplicate relationships. Cross-references are how adjacency is preserved without breaking the one-page-per-entity rule.
44|
45|### 2. Compiled Truth + Timeline (Two-Layer Pages)
46|
47|Every brain page has two layers, separated by a horizontal rule (`---`):
48|
49|**Above the line — Compiled Truth.** Always current, always rewritten when new information arrives. Starts with a one-paragraph executive summary. If you read only this, you know the state of play. Followed by structured State fields, Open Threads (active items — removed when resolved), and See Also (cross-links).
50|
51|**Below the line — Timeline.** Append-only, never rewritten. Reverse-chronological evidence log. Each entry: date, source, what happened. When an open thread gets resolved, it moves here with its resolution.
52|
53|If someone asks "what's the current state?" — read above the line. If someone asks "what happened?" — read below the line. The top is the current summary. The bottom is the source log.
54|
55|This is the Karpathy wiki pattern's killer feature: **the synthesis is pre-computed.** Unlike RAG, where the LLM re-derives knowledge from scratch every query, your brain has already done the work. The cross-references are already there. The contradictions have already been flagged.
56|
57|### 3. Enrichment Fires on Every Signal
58|
59|Every time any signal touches a person or company — meeting, email, tweet, calendar event, contact sync, conversation mention — the enrichment pipeline fires. The brain grows as a side effect of normal operations, not as a separate task you remember to do.
60|
61|This is what distinguishes an operational brain from Karpathy's research wiki. He describes ingesting sources you manually add. An operational brain goes further — every pipeline (meetings, email, social media, contacts) automatically triggers enrichment on every entity it touches. You never have to remember to update someone's page. The system does it because the plumbing is wired correctly.
62|
63|## Wiring It Into Your Agent
64|
65|The brain must be referenced in your agent's configuration (AGENTS.md or equivalent) as a hard rule, not a suggestion. Specifically:
66|
67|1. **Before creating any brain page → read RESOLVER.md.** This should be in your agent's operational rules, not buried in documentation.
68|2. **Before answering any question about people, companies, deals, or strategy → search the brain first.** Even if the agent thinks it knows the answer. File contents are current; the agent's memory of them goes stale.
69|3. **The enrich skill fires on every signal.** Every ingest pathway — meeting processing, email triage, social monitoring, contact sync — should call the enrichment pipeline when it encounters a person or company. This is wiring, not discipline. If it depends on the agent remembering, it will eventually be forgotten.
70|4. **Corrections are the highest-value data.** If the user corrects the agent about a person, company, deal, or decision — it gets written to the brain immediately. No batching, no deferring.
71|
72|The chain of authority: **Agent config (AGENTS.md) says "read RESOLVER.md" → RESOLVER.md is the decision tree → each directory README.md is the local resolver → schema.md defines page structure → the enrich skill defines the enrichment protocol.**
73|
74|## Architecture
75|
76|Three layers:
77|
78|**Raw sources** — meeting transcripts, emails, tweets, web research, API responses, calendar events, contact data. Immutable. The agent reads from these but never modifies them. Stored in `sources/` and `.raw/` sidecar directories.
79|
80|**The brain** — a directory of interlinked markdown files. People pages, company pages, deal pages, meeting pages, project pages, concept pages. The agent owns this layer entirely. It creates pages, updates them when new information arrives, maintains cross-references, and keeps everything consistent. You read it; the agent writes it.
81|
82|**The schema** — a document (this one, plus `schema.md` and `RESOLVER.md`) that tells the agent how the brain is structured, what the conventions are, and what workflows to follow. This is the key configuration file — it makes your agent a disciplined knowledge maintainer rather than a generic chatbot.
83|
84|## The Database + Markdown Architecture
85|
86|The markdown wiki is the human-facing layer — the primary interface for humans and LLMs. But it's not the sole source of truth. A structured database layer provides the foundation, and the markdown is generated from it.
87|
88|### The Four Database Primitives
89|
90|**Entity registry** — canonical ID, all aliases, all external IDs (LinkedIn member ID, X user ID, email addresses, phone numbers) in one table. This is the single source of truth for "is this the same person?" When you merge two entities, it's a database operation (point both IDs at the same canonical record), not a file-merge operation with cross-reference fixups.
91|
92|**Event ledger** — every signal that touches the brain is an immutable event: meeting attended, email received, tweet published, enrichment completed, user correction applied. Events have provenance: source, timestamp, confidence, raw payload reference. The timeline section of markdown pages is generated from this ledger. You never lose events because a page rewrite went wrong.
93|
94|**Fact store** — structured claims with provenance. "Jane Doe is CTO of Acme" with `source=crustdata, confidence=high, observed_at=2026-04-07`. When two sources disagree (LinkedIn says CTO, company website says VP Engineering), the conflict is visible as two facts for the same field with different values. The compiled truth section above the line is generated from the fact store's latest-confident values. Contradictions become data, not bugs.
95|
96|**Relationship graph** — typed edges between entities. Person→Company (role: CTO, started: 2024-01), Person→Person (relationship: co-founded company together), Company→Deal (type: Series A, date: 2025-03). Enables graph queries that markdown grep can't answer: "who do I know who's invested in AI infrastructure companies?" becomes a traversal, not a prayer.
97|
98|### Why This Matters
99|
100|- **Identity resolution** becomes a database operation (merge entity IDs), not a file-merge operation with manual cross-reference fixups
101|- **Contradictions are structural** (two facts with different values for the same field and different sources) rather than textual (hoping the LLM notices a discrepancy buried in prose)
102|- **Concurrency is solved** — events append to a ledger, facts upsert to a store, markdown is rebuilt. No more merge conflicts on shared files
103|- **Graph queries work** — "who do I know at this company?" and "what companies has this investor backed that I also know the founders of?" become database queries, not impossible grep chains
104|
105|### File-Layer Conventions
106|
107|The markdown layer uses conventions that map directly to the database primitives:
108|
109|1. **Use frontmatter for structured metadata** — anything you'd want to filter on (role, company, stage, score, tags) goes in YAML frontmatter, not buried in prose. Frontmatter is metadata for filters and schema-pack rules: it is not written to the fact store, and `gbrain search` / `query` do not index scalar frontmatter values (only the page body is chunked). If a value must be findable by search, also state it in the body, for example `Stage: negotiation` (#5335).
110|2. **Use `.raw/` for provenance** — save every API response with source and timestamp. These map to provenance records in the fact store.
111|3. **Treat the timeline as an event stream** — dated, sourced, append-only. These map to the event ledger.
112|4. **Keep compiled truth conceptually separate from evidence** — above the line is synthesis; below the line is evidence. The synthesis is a generated view; the evidence is queryable records.
113|5. **Use canonical slugs consistently** — every cross-reference uses the filename slug. These are the entity IDs in the registry.
114|
115|## Directory Structure
116|
117|```
118|brain/
119|├── RESOLVER.md        — master decision tree for filing (agent reads this first)
120|├── schema.md          — page conventions, templates, workflows
121|├── index.md           — content catalog with one-line summaries
122|├── log.md             — chronological record of all ingests/updates
123|├── people/            — one page per human being
124|│   ├── README.md      — resolver: what goes here, what doesn't
125|│   └── .raw/          — raw API responses per person (JSON sidecars)
126|├── companies/         — one page per organization
127|│   ├── README.md
128|│   └── .raw/
129|├── deals/             — financial transactions with terms and decisions
130|│   └── README.md
131|├── meetings/          — records of specific events with transcripts
132|│   └── README.md
133|├── projects/          — things being actively built (has a repo, spec, or team)
134|│   └── README.md
135|├── ideas/             — raw possibilities nobody is building yet
136|│   └── README.md
137|├── concepts/          — mental models and frameworks you'd teach
138|│   └── README.md
139|├── writing/           — prose artifacts (essays, philosophy, drafts)
140|│   └── README.md
141|├── programs/          — major life workstreams (the forest, not the trees)
142|│   └── README.md
143|├── org/               — your institution's strategy and operations
144|│   └── README.md
145|├── civic/             — political landscape, policy, government
146|│   └── README.md
147|├── media/             — public narrative, content ops, social monitoring
148|│   └── README.md
149|├── personal/          — private notes, health, personal reflections
150|│   └── README.md
151|├── household/         — domestic operations, properties, logistics
152|│   └── README.md
153|├── hiring/            — candidate pipelines and evaluations
154|│   └── README.md
155|├── sources/           — raw data imports and archived snapshots
156|│   └── README.md
157|├── prompts/           — reusable LLM prompt library
158|├── inbox/             — unsorted quick captures (temporary)
159|└── archive/           — dead pages, historical record
160|```
161|
162|Every directory has a README.md resolver. Adapt directories to your life — add or remove domains as needed. Not everyone needs civic/ or hiring/ or household/. The invariant is: **one directory per knowledge domain, one file per entity, every directory has a resolver, and RESOLVER.md is the master decision tree that guarantees MECE filing.**
163|
164|## Entity Identity and Deduplication
165|
166|In a system fed by meetings, email, social media, contacts, and APIs, **entity identity is the first real failure mode.** Without a canonical identity layer, you will end up with subtle split-brain pages — "Jane Smith" from a meeting transcript and "J. Smith" from an email and "jsmith" from Twitter all creating separate pages for the same person.
167|
168|### Canonical slugs
169|
170|Every entity gets a canonical slug that serves as its stable ID:
171|- People: `first-last.md` (all lowercase, hyphens for spaces)
172|- Companies: `company-name.md`
173|- If collisions arise, disambiguate: `david-liu-crustdata.md`, `david-liu-meta.md`
174|
175|The filename IS the identity. All references, cross-links, and .raw/ sidecars use this slug.
176|
177|### Aliases
178|
179|People have many names across sources. The frontmatter `aliases` field captures all known variants:
180|
181|```yaml
182|aliases: ["Jenny Shao", "Jenny G. Shao", "JennyGShao", "jennifer.shao@company.com"]
183|```
184|
185|Aliases include: misspellings from meeting transcripts, maiden names, nicknames, email addresses, social handles, and phonetic variants. When the enrich skill encounters a new name variant for a known entity, it adds the variant to aliases — it does NOT create a new page.
186|
187|Phone numbers are not aliases. A connector-rendered person page (Google Contacts) carries them under `phones:` in E.164 form, as exact identifiers for a deliberate `entity_identity_link` join; a digit string in `aliases` would match mentions it has nothing to do with.
188|
189|### Deduplication protocol
190|
191|Before creating any new page, the agent must:
192|1. Search existing pages by name (exact and fuzzy)
193|2. Search aliases across all pages: `grep -rl "NAME_VARIANT" /data/brain/people/ --include="*.md"`
194|3. Check .raw/ sidecars for matching email addresses or social handles
195|4. If a match is found → UPDATE the existing page (add alias if the name variant is new)
196|5. If no match → CREATE a new page
197|
198|### Merge protocol
199|
200|When you discover two pages are the same person:
201|1. Pick the more complete page as the survivor
202|2. Merge all timeline entries from the duplicate into the survivor (chronological order)
203|3. Merge all aliases
204|4. Update all cross-references that pointed to the duplicate
205|5. Delete the duplicate
206|6. Commit with message: `merge: [duplicate] into [survivor]`
207|
208|During weekly lint, actively look for potential duplicates: similar names, same company, same email across different pages.
209|
210|## Key Disambiguation Rules
211|
212|The most common filing confusions and how to resolve them:
213|
214|- **Concept vs. Idea:** Could you *teach* it as a framework? → concept. Could you *build* it? → idea.
215|- **Concept vs. Personal:** Would you share it in a professional talk? → concept. Is it private reflection? → personal.
216|- **Idea vs. Project:** Is anyone working on it? Yes → project. No → idea. The graduation moment is when work starts.
217|- **Writing vs. Media:** Writing is the *artifact* (the essay). Media is the *production and distribution infrastructure* (content pipeline, social monitoring).
218|- **Writing vs. Concepts:** A concept page is distilled (200 words of compiled truth). An essay is developed prose (argument, narrative, story).
219|- **Person vs. Company:** Is it about *them as a human*? → people/. Is it about *the organization*? → companies/. Both pages link to each other.
220|- **Household vs. Personal:** Would a PA execute on it? → household (operational). Is it private reflection? → personal.
221|- **Sources vs. .raw/ sidecars:** Per-entity enrichment data → .raw/ sidecar. Bulk multi-entity imports → sources/.
222|
223|When nothing fits, file in inbox/ and flag it. That's a signal the schema needs to evolve.
224|
225|## Page Types and Templates
226|
227|### Person
228|
229|The most important page type. A great person page is a well-researched briefing — not a LinkedIn scrape.

Usage: gbrain put <slug> [options]
       gbrain put <slug> [options] < file   (--content read from stdin)

Complete content REPLACES the whole page: read get_page include_content:true; its revision is expected_revision. Keep a request_id UUID; retry with identical arguments. 2|name: brain-ops
3|version: 1.2.0
4|upstream: brain-ops@fc834ee
5|description: |
6|  Brain knowledge base operations. The core read/write cycle: brain-first lookup,
7|  read-enrich-write loop, source attribution, ambient enrichment, back-linking.
8|  Read this before any brain interaction.
9|triggers:
10|  - any brain read/write/lookup/citation
11|tools:
12|  - recall
13|  - search
14|  - query
15|  - get_page
16|  - put_page
17|  - add_link
18|  - add_timeline_entry
19|  - get_backlinks
20|  - sync_brain
21|mutating: true
22|writes_pages: true
23|writes_to:
24|  - people/
25|  - companies/
26|  - deals/
27|  - concepts/
28|  - meetings/
29|---
30|
31|# Brain Operations — The Ambient Context Layer
32|
33|Recall relevant context before responding. Save explicit requests with
34|provenance; automatic capture is off until the user opts in. Reading this skill
35|does not enable capture, delegation, or paid enrichment. A chat-only instruction
36|suppresses writes for that turn, including when standing capture is enabled.
37|
38|> **Convention:** See `skills/conventions/brain-first.md` for the lookup chain and copyable retrieval filters.
39|> **Convention:** See `skills/conventions/quality.md` for citation and back-link rules.
40|
41|## Contract
42|
43|This skill guarantees:
44|- Brain is checked BEFORE any external API call (brain-first lookup)
45|- Explicit save requests and opted-in inbound signals trigger the READ → WRITE
46|  loop; enrichment requires its separately configured authority
47|- Every outbound response checks brain for relevant context
48|- Source attribution on every fact written (inline `[Source: ...]` citations)
49|- User's direct statements are highest-authority data
50|- Back-links maintained on every brain write (Iron Law)
51|
52|**Iron Law:** every mention of a person or company with a brain page gets a
53|back-link FROM that entity's page TO the page mentioning them.
54|
55|## Read
56|
57|Before any external lookup of a person, company or topic:
58|
59|1. `gbrain entity "<name>"` — one call for a known entity: description,
60|   aliases, open threads, recent events, edges. Near-misses return suggestions.
61|2. `gbrain search "name"` for exact tokens; `gbrain query "question"` for
62|   concepts (a nonzero `search` count is not proof of completeness).
63|3. `gbrain get <slug>`, `gbrain backlinks <slug>`, `gbrain timeline <slug>`.
64|4. `gbrain think "<question>"` only for paid multi-page synthesis ("what
65|   changed since Q1"); `query` is enough to find a page.
66|
67|External APIs fill gaps; they never start the lookup. Answer from the brain
68|page when one exists, and cite it.
69|
70|**Count with gbrain, not `ls`.** Corpora nest (`meetings/YYYY/MM/` beside a
71|flat layer), so a shallow `ls dir/*.md` undercounts. Use `gbrain sources list`,
72|`gbrain list --type <t>`, or `find <dir> -name '*.md' | wc -l`.
73|
74|## Write (only when authorized)
75|
76|Write for an explicit save request, or a message inside the user's opted-in
77|capture scope with no chat-only restriction. Otherwise use the information in
78|this conversation without persisting it; explicit remembering does not enable
79|ongoing capture.
80|
81|1. Detect entities; read their pages first. Before creating a page, check for
82|   it (`gbrain entity`, then `query` with name variants) — never duplicate.
83|2. Write only what is new, with `[Source: User, YYYY-MM-DD]` (or the real
84|   source) on each fact, plus a timeline entry
85|   (`gbrain timeline-add <slug> <date> "<text>"`) on every entity involved.
86|3. Never overwrite the user's direct statements with lower-authority sources.
87|4. Confirm a write only after reading it back.
88|
89|**Memory verbs (MEMORY_VERBS v1).** `remember(fact, provenance)` saves one formed
90|fact (CLI: `gbrain remember "<fact>" --entity <slug> --provenance "<who, date>"`);
91|`recall`, `entity`, `synthesize`, `context_pack` and `delta` read.
92|`forget(id)` (`gbrain forget <fact-id>`) withdraws a fact from active memory;
93|history, source material and backups may remain, so never promise erasure.
94|`put_page` / `add_link` / `add_timeline_entry` stay the page and graph path.
95|Contract: `docs/protocol/MEMORY_VERBS_v1.md`.
96|
97|**Keyless brains:** when `extract_facts` returns `skipped: extraction_unavailable`
98|(or `extraction_failed` for one turn), you are the extractor: write each fact
99|with `remember`, setting `kind` (event | preference | commitment | belief |
100|fact) and the visibility the envelope's `agent_action` names (default private;
101|`remember` defaults to world, or to your own member page when your credential
102|is bound to a member other than the brain owner).
103|
104|**Visibility.** Every MCP caller (stdio included) and a thin CLI recall and
105|withdraw world-visible facts only; private recall needs the trusted local CLI
106|or a credential bound to the brain owner (`gbrain access owner`).
107|Never widen visibility or request broader OAuth scopes to make a check pass.
108|An MCP connection test uses only a harmless synthetic `visibility: "world"`
109|fact, withdrawn afterward.
110|
111|**`<REDACTED:pattern>`** in a result means the brain withheld a credential-shaped
112|value; the page is unchanged and `gbrain recall` on the brain host shows it.
113|Say which kind was withheld; never retry to recover it or guess it.
114|
115|**Tight-budget page questions:**
116|`gbrain recall --query '<q>' --budget-tokens 75 --budget-policy query_first --json`
117|packs page evidence before recent facts (`skills/query/SKILL.md`). Read
118|`budget_packing` before calling an empty result missing memory.
119|
120|### Auto-link
121|
122|Trusted local writes (`gbrain put`, `gbrain capture`, `gbrain call put_page`)
123|auto-link inline and return `auto_links: { created, removed, errors }`. MCP
124|writes (stdio and HTTP) return `auto_links: { skipped: "remote" }`: body
125|wikilinks are saved as text and a post-commit effect queues plain `mentions`
126|edges to existing pages (`gbrain config set mcp.remote_auto_links off` turns it
127|off). Typed, frontmatter and timeline edges wait for a sweep: stdio
128|`gbrain serve` runs one at startup and when idle; `gbrain serve --http` does not self-sweep, so run
129|`gbrain sweep --once` or `gbrain extract links --source db`. Use `add_link` for
130|a relationship you need now, except meeting attendance, which comes from the
131|meeting page's attendee list. Dated events still need `gbrain timeline-add`.
132|`gbrain config set auto_link false` disables auto-link.
133|
134|## Enrichment
135|
136|External research, paid calls and delegation need their own authority: an
137|explicit enrichment request or the user's stored scope and spending policy. A
138|mentioned entity, a shared link or capture opt-in is not that authority. Never
139|block the response on enrichment.
140|
141|## Output Format
142|
143|Answer with the retrieved context and cite it. With several sources, cite
144|`[source-id:slug]` using the `source_id` every page payload carries (never the
145|source's display name); a single-source brain may write `[default:slug]` or the
146|bare slug. Confirm authorized writes only after readback; if no write was
147|requested or opted in, do not persist the conversation to produce a memory update.
148|
149|## When it fails
150|
151|Follow the [agent operator protocol](../conventions/agent-operator-protocol.md) for any gbrain error `code`, exit code, `[AGENT]` block or notice block. Specific to this skill:
152|
153|- `revision_conflict`: re-read, merge your change into the new text, save with the new revision. `write_pending` (exit 10): poll `gbrain write-request <request_id>` before claiming the write landed.
154|- `owner_unavailable` with `detail: unbound_source` (classic Postgres brain): write the file in the source's checkout, commit, and run `gbrain sync --source <id>`; if you are remote, give the user those steps. Never claim the source or switch modes (see the [agent operator protocol](../conventions/agent-operator-protocol.md#a-write-refused-owner_unavailable-with-detail-unbound_source)).
155|- `permission_denied` from the secret scan or a slug fence: do not strip or rename to dodge it; tell the user what was refused and why (`docs/guides/write-refusals.md`).
156|- Empty `recall` / `search` with a degraded notice or `search_degraded`: say the brain is searching keywords only right now, not that nothing is saved.
157|- `insufficient_scope` / `scope_denied` over MCP: tell the user; never ask for a broader token to make a write pass.
158|
159|## Anti-Patterns
160|
161|- Answering about people or companies from general knowledge, or calling external APIs, before checking the brain
162|- Writing facts without `[Source: ...]`, or without the back-links and timeline entries
163|- Creating a duplicate page, or a page for a non-notable entity
164|- Writing to the brain without a save request or capture opt-in
165|- Promising that `forget` erases a fact everywhere", "total_lines": 165, "file_size": 8459, "truncated": false, "is_binary": false, "is_image": false}

{"content": "321|silently, and don't stop the install to ask either: on every harness, connect
322|gbrain first (with `gbrain setup <harness>` or the `harness_wiring` step), then
323|show the matrix and the applied mode in the reply that reports the install, as
324|a choice the user can make at any time, and run
325|`gbrain config set search.mode <mode>` when they pick one.
326|
327|If you already know the operator's choice, record it at install time instead:
328|`gbrain init --search-mode <conservative|balanced|tokenmax>` stores it as the
329|operator's (`search.mode_source: operator`) and init asks no `search_mode`
330|question. On an existing brain with a different mode it refuses unless you pass
331|`--force`.
332|
333|**Present this matrix verbatim:**
334|
335|<!-- Cost matrix: generated by costMatrixLines() in src/core/search/mode-advice.ts (prices from src/core/model-pricing.ts); test/init-mode-picker.test.ts keeps this block in sync. -->
336|```
337|Estimated downstream input cost of the retrieved payload @ 10K queries/mo:
338|
339|                  Haiku 5.5     Sonnet 5.5    Opus 5.5
340|                  ($0.10/M in)  ($2/M in)     ($4/M in)
341|  conservative    $4/mo         $80/mo        $160/mo
342|  balanced        $10/mo        $200/mo       $400/mo
343|  tokenmax        $20/mo        $400/mo       $800/mo
344|
345|  Assumed payload per query: conservative 4K, balanced 10K, tokenmax 20K tokens.
346|  Scales linearly: x10 for 100K queries/mo, /10 for 1K. 200x corner-to-corner spread.
347|  Embedding, reranking and query expansion are separate provider charges.
348|```
349|
350|**Ask the operator (paraphrase if needed):**
351|
352|> Your gbrain is installed and connected, with search mode
353|> `<auto-applied default>`. It controls retrieval payload size, and you can
354|> change it any time. The modes:
355|>
356|>   1) conservative — tight 4K budget, 10 chunks max, no reranker.
